catalog_quote: Unlike the segmental elements and tone, stress in Qh is predictable always by rule, and never serves to differentiate lexical meanings or categories. It is assigned at the utterance level, and is manifested phonetically as the lengthening of the penultimate syllable of the utterance. The presence of a penultimately lengthened syllable at the end of an utterance indicates that the speaker is about to pause or stop speaking altogether. It also generally signals the neutral attitude (for example, non-surprised, non-angry etc.) of the speaker, and that the sentence-type is a statement, or possibly a non-urgent imperative (that is, one for whose fulfilment the speaker does not require urgent action). Citation forms are also neutral utterances and they too are assigned penultimate length. In other utterance-types (for example, urgent imperatives and questions), or where nc [sic] break occurs in the utterance, stress does not occur, and all syllables are of the same, short, duration. The description of stressing given above has been put in fairly categorical terms, but it should be borne in mind that no detailed analysis of stressing was carried out in running speech. For this reason we consider it premature to attempt a formalization of the stress assignment rule, although for convenience we will refer to this rule as Prepausal Penultimate Lengthening (PPL).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kgalagadi is a two-tone (H/L) language. 'Stress' is non-contrastive and is assigned at the utterance level: it is realised as lengthening of the penultimate syllable of a pre-pausal (declarative, non-urgent-imperative, citation-form) utterance, i.e. Bantu-type Prepausal Penultimate Lengthening. Utterance-medial words and question/urgent-imperative utterances carry no stress; all syllables are then equally short. In a word said in isolation the penult is therefore the prominent syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: No stress (no penultimate lengthening) in questions, urgent imperatives, and where no break occurs in the utterance. Dickens adds that no detailed analysis of stressing in running speech was carried out and calls a formalisation premature (p. 22). Hyman & Monaka 2008 (pp. 272, 284) and Crane 2009 (p. 226) confirm PLL as a phrase-level, pre-pausal declarative process, suspended in questions, imperatives and ideophones, with no lexical length contrast.
new_statements.domain_note: Utterance/phrase domain, not the word: prominence falls on the penult of the pre-pausal phrase; citation forms (isolated words) are explicitly included, so word-in-isolation = penultimate. Dickens's data: Qhalaxarzi of Kacgae and Lone Tree (Ghanzi District, Botswana; 'Sjaxa dialect') plus Sekoma and Letlhakeng speakers, 1975-1984.
new_statements.identity_note: Dickens 1986 describes 'Qhalaxarzi' = Shekgalagari (Glottolog lists Qhalaxarzi as an alternate name of kgal1244), from speakers at Kacgae and Lone Tree (Ghanzi District, western Botswana; Dickens calls it the 'Sjaxa dialect') and at Sekoma and Letlhakeng (Kweneng), 1975-1984. Gunnink 2022 describes the divergent northern Shetjhauba variety (Okavango panhandle), which has no separate glottocode that I could see; Monaka 2023 and Crane 2009 / Hyman & Monaka 2008 describe standard/central Shekgalagari. All agree on non-contrastive pre-pausal penultimate lengthening.

sources.note: Section 2.5 'Stress' (pp. 21-22, PDF pp. 37-38; verified against page image): stress is always predictable by rule, never contrastive, assigned at the utterance level and realised as lengthening of the utterance-penultimate syllable ('Prepausal Penultimate Lengthening', PPL); citation forms get it too; in questions, urgent imperatives and utterance-medially there is no stress and all syllables are short. Two phonemic tones H and L (2.6.0).

As this process is not contrastive, penultimate lengthening is not indicated in the examples'; §2.2 Tones: two contrastive tones H and L, falling tones only on the lengthened penult. sources.citation: Hyman, Larry M. & Kemmonye C. Monaka. 2008. Tonal and non-tonal intonation in Shekgalagari. UC Berkeley Phonology Lab Annual Report 4: 269-288. DOI 10.5070/P74429729r (preprint of Hyman & Monaka 2011, Springer)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Does not use 'stress' for Shekgalagari. Describes penultimate lengthening + L% ('PLL') as declarative/pre-pausal intonation; p. 272: 'Two contour tones, HL and L↓L, occur only on a lengthened penultimate syllable'; p. 284: 'there is no underlying lexical contrast [in length] in the language', and quotes Hyman 1978 on Bantu 'superimposed penultimate accent'. PLL suspended in questions, urgent imperatives, ideophones.
